question: When sparse autoencoders scale to wider dictionaries, do they discover proportionally more underlying features, or can they spend most new latents tiling a few common multidimensional feature manifolds?

key_findings.claim: Under the paper's allocation model, SAE scaling has a sharp asymptotic regime change determined by the feature-frequency exponent alpha and per-feature approximation exponent beta.
key_findings.evidence: With feature frequency p_i proportional to i^-(1+alpha) and loss L_i(n) proportional to n^-beta, alpha less than beta yields loss N^-alpha and linear feature discovery D(N) proportional to N. When beta is less than alpha, loss instead follows N^-beta and discovery is sublinear, D(N) proportional to N^((1+beta)/(1+alpha)).

key_findings.claim: The regime result depends on a strong reduction of SAE training to independent per-feature latent allocation.
key_findings.evidence: The derivation assumes every latent fires for only one feature, each decoder direction stays in that feature's subspace, feature subspaces are orthogonal, sparsity penalties are separable, and optimization reaches the best allocation. The authors explicitly note that feature absorption and nonorthogonality violate these premises in practice.

key_findings.claim: A single slowly approximated common manifold can absorb most dictionary growth in the numerical allocation model.
key_findings.evidence: The simulation combines one power-law-loss manifold with otherwise discrete features and Zipf-like frequencies. In the beta-less-than-alpha case, a nominal 100-million-latent SAE discovers only about 3 million features because the common manifold receives most marginal capacity.

key_findings.claim: Toy SAE loss curves are highly geometry-dependent, and radial variation produces the strongest reported evidence against the proposed pathology.
key_findings.evidence: ReLU and JumpReLU SAEs can keep lowering loss by tiling hollow hyperspheres, with dimensions 6-8 showing an estimated beta near 0.05 over 10^2 to 10^4 latents. When radius varies from 0.5 to 2, loss instead plateaus near roughly twice the intrinsic dimension, consistent with positive and negative basis directions rather than indefinite tiling.

key_findings.claim: The real-model probes do not establish that practical language-model SAEs are in the pathological regime.
key_findings.evidence: Gemma Scope latent firing ranks have fitted slopes between -0.57 and -0.74, but the paper explains that absorption, composition, and manifold tiling make these poor estimators of true feature frequencies. Most Gemma decoder directions lack extremely close neighbors; the few pairs above 0.97 often include a dead latent. Inception-v1 SAEs show more close directions, but duplicated atoms under L1 are an alternative explanation.

key_findings.claim: The paper is primarily a falsifiable framing rather than an empirical diagnosis of deployed SAE scaling.
key_findings.evidence: The discussion states that neither the true feature-frequency distribution nor real feature-manifold geometry is known, and that the work does not resolve whether practical SAEs occupy the pathological regime. No ground-truth multi-feature real activation benchmark measures D(N) directly.

method.core_idea: Adapt a neural capacity-allocation scaling model so that SAE width is divided among sparsely occurring discrete or manifold-valued features, then derive when loss minimization favors new-feature discovery versus repeated refinement of common manifolds.
method.mechanism: Activations are modeled as sums of orthogonal feature-subspace samples. Given feature-specific latents, the expected SAE reconstruction-plus-sparsity loss decomposes into p_i L_i(n_i), with a fixed total latent budget. A continuous Lagrange-multiplier allocation for power-law feature frequencies and per-feature losses yields the two asymptotic regimes. ReLU and JumpReLU SAEs trained on synthetic spheres and radial shells probe candidate L_i curves; firing-frequency ranks and decoder nearest-neighbor cosines supply preliminary real-model diagnostics.
assumptions: Each semantic feature occupies a fixed linear subspace and appears sparsely.
Every learned SAE latent is specific to exactly one underlying feature.
Decoder atoms assigned to a feature remain inside its subspace.
SAE optimization reaches the globally best latent allocation and can be summarized only by n_i.
Feature frequencies and per-feature approximation losses obey stable power laws.
Continuous allocation and a one-latent discovery cutoff accurately approximate discrete SAE dictionaries.
Synthetic sphere and radial-shell geometry brackets relevant geometry in neural activations.

techniques.role: Rewrites expected SAE loss as independent feature losses under a shared latent budget.
Derives loss and feature-discovery exponents from alpha and beta.
Visualizes how extra ReLU atoms partition a circular feature into narrow activation arcs.
Measures how ReLU and JumpReLU reconstruction loss changes with width on hollow and radially varying manifolds.
Uses Gemma Scope activation-frequency slopes as a tentative proxy for feature-frequency decay.
Searches real SAE dictionaries for clusters of nearly collinear atoms expected under manifold tiling.

evaluations.setting: Analytic allocation with p_i proportional to i^-(1+alpha) and common L_i(n) proportional to n^-beta.
evaluations.metric: Total loss exponent and discovered-feature count D(N).
evaluations.result: Linear discovery when alpha is below beta; sublinear N^((1+beta)/(1+alpha)) discovery when beta is below alpha.
evaluations.baseline: Discrete one-dimensional features, for which one new latent discovers one new feature.

evaluations.setting: Numerical allocation with one common power-law-loss manifold and all remaining features discrete.
evaluations.metric: Latents assigned per feature and D(N) through dictionary width 100 million.
evaluations.result: In the pathological parameter regime, only roughly 3 million features are discovered at 100 million latents.

evaluations.setting: ReLU L1 and JumpReLU SAEs trained for 12,000 Adam steps on unit hyperspheres and radially varying shells.
evaluations.metric: Reconstruction-plus-sparsity loss versus SAE width and fitted beta.
evaluations.result: Hollow high-dimensional spheres retain slow improvement to at least 10,000 latents; radial shells plateau near about 2d_i atoms.
evaluations.baseline: Discrete features and hollow versus radially varying geometry.

evaluations.setting: Gemma Scope residual-stream SAEs and a 7,680-latent L1 SAE on Inception-v1 mixed3b activations.
evaluations.metric: Ranked firing frequency and nearest-neighbor decoder cosine.
evaluations.result: Gemma Scope shows few extremely close live pairs, while the vision SAE has a meaningful high-cosine fraction with duplication as a confounder.

limitations: Feature identity is latent and unobserved in real networks, so the central discovery count D(N) is not measured.
Orthogonal, independent feature subspaces exclude superposition, feature absorption, compositions, and cross-feature interactions.
The shared beta model suppresses heterogeneous geometry; the one-special-manifold simulation is illustrative rather than representative.
The exponent estimates from firing frequencies are not identifiable with true feature-frequency exponents.
Nearest-neighbor cosine cannot distinguish manifold tiling from duplicate atoms, dead latents, correlated concepts, or optimization artifacts.
Synthetic experiments use simple spheres and shells, not measured local manifolds from language-model activations.
No downstream interpretability, causal fidelity, rare-feature recall, or circuit-recovery metric tests whether lower reconstruction loss is harmful.
failure_modes: Nonorthogonal features can share decoder atoms, invalidating additive loss and the notion of a unique allocation n_i.
Optimization may produce dead, duplicated, absorbed, or compositional latents rather than the globally optimal tiling assumed by the theory.
Apparent power laws can be finite-range crossovers, making the alpha-beta threshold extrapolation wrong at larger widths.
A manifold may ripple through ambient dimensions or change topology and local dimension, so a single L_i curve is insufficient.
High decoder cosine can overstate tiling, while curved manifolds represented by dissimilar tangent atoms can evade the diagnostic.
Reconstruction improvements on a common feature might preserve behaviorally important within-feature variation, so calling them pathological can be semantically wrong.
reusable_insights: Track how a larger representation allocates capacity, not only how aggregate reconstruction loss scales.
Distinguish feature count from latent count; overcomplete dictionaries need not deliver one semantic unit per coordinate.
Use geometry-controlled synthetic data to expose objective-induced tiling before interpreting real latents.
Report rare-feature recall or ground-truth factor coverage alongside reconstruction and sparsity.
Treat radial variation, intrinsic dimension, and curvature as separate determinants of dictionary scaling.
Audit dead and duplicated atoms before interpreting high cosine as evidence of a semantic manifold.
open_questions: Can controlled generative activation benchmarks with known multidimensional factors measure D(N) directly across SAE widths?
What are the local dimension, curvature, radial variation, and feature-frequency distributions of real transformer activations?
Can a nonorthogonal allocation theory include superposition, feature absorption, and shared decoder atoms?
Would subspace-, mixture-, polynomial-, or manifold-aware decoders discover rare factors more efficiently than linear SAEs?
Can interventions distinguish harmless within-feature tiling from wasted duplicates and from important fine-grained structure?
Do cross-layer and cross-model scaling exponents prospectively predict where wider SAEs cease to improve feature coverage?

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling and Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders
competitive_landscape.relationship: The principal empirical SAE scaling-law predecessor.
competitive_landscape.difference: It fits reconstruction and sparsity scaling across SAE size and training compute; the reviewed paper supplies a capacity-allocation interpretation and argues that the same loss scaling may conceal sublinear semantic feature discovery.

competitive_landscape.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct empirical motivation for multidimensional feature geometry in language models.
competitive_landscape.difference: It identifies and evaluates multidimensional features in real activations; the reviewed paper assumes such features and studies how their approximation-loss curves could distort SAE width scaling.

competitive_landscape.title: Projecting Assumptions: The Duality Between Sparse Autoencoders and Concept Geometry
competitive_landscape.relationship: Close analysis of how SAE architectural assumptions select only certain concept geometries.
competitive_landscape.difference: It develops geometry-dependent recovery biases and motivates new architectures; the reviewed paper focuses specifically on asymptotic capacity allocation and the risk that common manifolds absorb dictionary width.

competitive_landscape.title: The Geometric Wall: Manifold Structure Predicts Layerwise Sparse Autoencoder Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later, direct empirical competitor connecting activation-manifold geometry to SAE scaling across layers.
competitive_landscape.difference: It regresses scaling behavior across 844 Gemma Scope checkpoints and tests layerwise geometry predictors, whereas the reviewed paper offers an analytic regime model plus small synthetic and nearest-neighbor probes. This later work raises the evidential bar for claims about real-world pathological scaling.

competitive_landscape.title: Decomposing the Dark Matter of Sparse Autoencoders
competitive_landscape.relationship: Empirical investigation of what remains in SAE reconstruction error and how that error affects model loss.
competitive_landscape.difference: It measures nonlinear error structure and downstream cross-entropy consequences; the reviewed paper theorizes missing feature discovery from dictionary allocation but does not inspect SAE residuals or behavioral impact directly.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a formal explanation for how multidimensional feature manifolds can make SAE loss scale smoothly while the number of discovered features grows far more slowly than dictionary width.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Sections 2.2-2.6 and Appendix B adapt the Brill capacity-allocation derivation; Sections 3 and E provide synthetic and preliminary real-dictionary probes.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The alpha-versus-beta discovery-regime framing is a crisp and reusable contribution, particularly because it separates loss scaling from feature coverage. Its real-world conclusion is intentionally unresolved and rests on restrictive identifiability and orthogonality assumptions. Prior work already established SAE scaling, multidimensional features, geometric recovery bias, and dark residual structure; later cross-layer work tests the geometry-scaling link more directly.

reviewer_notes: Read all 13 extracted pages, including derivations, synthetic details, and real-dictionary appendices. Primary-source searches covered empirical SAE scaling, multidimensional features, geometry-aware critiques, residual dark matter, and the closest 2026 cross-layer follow-up. The review preserves the paper's own conclusion that practical pathological scaling is not established.
